analysis.title: The AI diversification dilemma
key_insights: Nuveen estimates $5.5 trillion to $6.0 trillion will be required for AI investment through 2030, with around 80% financed through capital markets, predominantly credit.

Reducing exposure to the largest technology companies means underweights against concentrated benchmarks and may sacrifice returns if AI spending keeps accelerating. Keeping those holdings while adding AI-related credit and infrastructure adds exposure to the same cycle. Nuveen recommends keeping conviction in the AI theme while being more selective about where the risk is taken.

Traditional issuer and sector limits miss interconnected AI exposure. One hyperscaler can sit in a portfolio as equity, investment-grade credit, guarantor of a private data centre bond lease and anchor tenant of an infrastructure investment.

AI capex also supports semiconductor revenues, construction activity, electricity demand and repayment capacity of privately financed projects, so a spending slowdown would hit businesses with very different sector classifications.

The Magnificent 7 contributed around 52% of S&P 500 net earnings growth in 2024, and without them 2023 earnings growth would have been negative. Three Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers made up nearly one-third of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index at end of September 2026.

Nuveen proposes a portfolio-wide AI exposure budget built on sources of revenue and repayment. The stress case is a hyperscaler capex slowdown, with weaker chipmaker earnings and multiples and wider spreads on lease-backed data centre bonds. Losses are aggregated net of offsets and expressed in percentage points of portfolio value. A second, disorderly scenario assumes rising correlations and worse liquidity.

Diversifiers are harder to find because industrials and commodity producers are increasingly tied to data centre demand. Nuveen favours European and Japanese industrials that use AI for productivity over those that supply the infrastructure, often at more attractive valuations than U.S. tech leaders.

Nuveen favours capital-intensive infrastructure with hard-to-replicate assets and limited obsolescence risk, such as power grids, baseload generation and cooling systems. It also favours non-U.S. airports, toll roads, utilities and midstream pipelines, where AI-driven energy demand is not fully priced in.

Nuveen sees opportunities in European financials and old-economy businesses such as packaging. In private markets it favours core middle-market lending to old-economy businesses (wastewater management, commercial landscaping), health care real estate and grocery-anchored retail.

Benchmark-relative underperformance is possible if tech leadership continues. Nuveen favours accepting some benchmark-relative risk to build independent return sources while keeping meaningful AI participation.

As of July, nearly 80% of data centre securities issued since early 2025 were quoted at wider spreads than at issuance, and some planned bond sales were postponed or withdrawn. Investment grade data centre bonds trade 50 to 200 basis points wider than their tenants' unsecured debt, partly for construction risk, illiquidity and residual asset value uncertainty.

The largest tech platforms have conservative reported leverage, but over $1 trillion of leases not yet commenced and about $1.7 trillion of purchase commitments imply large future obligations. Circular financing lets stress in one part of the AI ecosystem reach counterparties elsewhere. Debt of lower-rated AI infrastructure providers, including data centre bonds leased to them, has weakened recently.

Execution risks include power constraints and local opposition that delay projects, raise financing costs and, under certain contract provisions, allow tenants to terminate leases, leaving lenders without the expected cash flows.

Nuveen favours select privately placed lease-backed and project bonds where pay reflects the risks. Better compensation addresses pricing, not correlation, since exposure to hyperscaler capex decisions remains.

In public credit Nuveen favours investment-grade utility operating companies, energy and power infrastructure financing, and established providers of power management, cooling and network infrastructure. Selective emerging market debt, especially Latin American local currency debt where real yields are attractive, offers return drivers less tied to AI.
Private market investors face liquidity risk because refinancing needs and capital calls could coincide across investments tied to the same technology counterparties.

Pressure is concentrated in lower-rated borrowers and projects under construction, which Nuveen reads as a reason for selectivity, not retreat. Hyperscaler debt spreads have also widened, but higher rates and heavy issuance appear to have mattered more than credit quality concerns.

Nuveen's view would change if pressure spreads beyond the vulnerable parts of the market, or if weaker fundamentals, capex guidance cuts or slowing cloud revenue growth emerge. Sustained cloud revenue growth and stronger AI monetization would reinforce the investment case.

sector_views.rationale: Capital-intensive, hard-to-replicate assets with limited obsolescence risk, high replacement cost and relatively inelastic demand.

sector_views.sector: Non-U.S. infrastructure (airports, toll roads, utilities, midstream pipelines)
sector_views.rationale: AI-driven energy demand not fully priced in, often at more attractive entry points than U.S. counterparts.
Earnings driven by different sources of demand than AI investment.
Exposed to weaker earnings and lower multiples if hyperscaler capex slows. Nuveen advises distinguishing infrastructure suppliers from AI users.
Contractual cash flows can support debt service.

earnings_insights: The Magnificent 7 contributed around 52% of S&P 500 total net earnings growth in 2024 (LSEG, reported). Without them, 2023 S&P 500 earnings growth would have been negative.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight select privately placed lease-backed and project bonds financing AI data centres, where compensation reflects construction and residual value risk
trade_ideas.rationale: These structures can offer more attractive terms than unsecured exposure to the same tenant.
trade_ideas.risk: Better compensation addresses pricing, not correlation, since exposure to hyperscaler capex remains.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight selective Latin American local currency emerging market debt where real yields are attractive
trade_ideas.rationale: Returns supported by domestic monetary policy and currency appreciation rather than technology earnings.

risk_factors: Hyperscaler capex slowdown hitting chipmaker earnings and multiples and widening lease-backed data centre bond spreads.
Rising correlations and falling liquidity across AI-linked assets in a disorderly scenario.
Circular financing arrangements spreading stress across AI ecosystem counterparties.
Weak tenant credit: over $1 trillion of leases not yet commenced and about $1.7 trillion of purchase commitments.
Construction delays from power constraints and local opposition, which can let tenants terminate leases.
Coinciding refinancing needs and capital calls in private market allocations tied to the same technology counterparties.
Benchmark-relative underperformance if technology leadership continues.
vol_and_positioning: Nuveen warns that correlations across AI-linked assets could rise and undermine the diversification investors expect from holding them in different parts of a portfolio.

tension_points.bull_case: Sustained cloud revenue growth and stronger evidence of AI monetization would reinforce the investment case. Tech leadership may continue, rewarding benchmark-aligned holders.
tension_points.bear_case: Portfolios diversified across asset classes are increasingly dependent on a few tech companies' spending. A capex slowdown would hit chipmakers, data centre bonds, utilities and private projects together, and correlations may rise.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Nuveen's selective stance would change if pressure spreads beyond lower-rated borrowers and projects under construction, or if capex guidance cuts or slowing cloud revenue growth appear.

theme_stances.key_argument: Portfolios diversified across asset classes and geographies are becoming more dependent on the spending decisions of a few technology companies.
theme_stances.evidence: more dependent on the spending decisions of a handful of technology companies

theme_stances.key_argument: Repricing creates opportunities for selective lenders if terms compensate for construction risk and give sufficient creditor protection.
theme_stances.evidence: The repricing creates opportunities for selective lenders
